title: RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE IN JERICHO—YET HER NAME ENTERED THE LINE OF CHRIST
paragraphs:
RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE IN JERICHO—YET HER NAME ENTERED THE LINE OF CHRIST
The woman a city could have remembered by her scandal became the woman Scripture remembers by her faith—and generations later, her name appeared in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
There are names people whisper.
Names attached to mistakes.
Names followed by a story nobody lets you forget.
Names that enter a room before the person does.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe nobody calls you by your old sin anymore, but you can still hear the accusation in your own head.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abused.
Promiscuous.
Drunk.
Liar.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Backslider.
Too dirty.
Too late.
Too far gone.
And sometimes the cruelest voice isn't coming from another person.
It is coming from inside you.
You can sit in church, sing about grace, hear sermons about forgiveness, and still secretly wonder whether Jesus really wants someone with your history.
Then you meet Rahab.
And suddenly the excuses begin to collapse.
Because Scripture does not introduce Rahab by hiding the uncomfortable part.
Joshua 2:1 describes her as אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishshah zonah — a woman who was a prostitute.
The Greek New Testament is equally direct.
Hebrews 11:31 calls her Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē — “Rahab the prostitute.”
James 2:25 uses the same identifying word, πόρνη (pornē).
The Bible does not airbrush her past.
But neither does God allow her past to have the final word.
And that difference is everything.
Rahab lived in Jericho.
Not outside the coming judgment.
Inside it.

Israel had crossed into the land, and Jericho stood in their path. Joshua sent two men to spy out the city. They entered Rahab's house, and soon the king of Jericho learned that Israelite spies had arrived.
Rahab was suddenly standing at a terrifying crossroads.
Protect the men of Israel and risk everything.
Or surrender them and remain aligned with the city in which she had built her life.
She hid them.
But what makes her story extraordinary is not merely that she hid two spies.
It is what came out of her mouth afterward.
She told them:
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
Then Rahab revealed something even deeper.
She had heard.
She had heard what the LORD had done at the Red Sea.
She had heard what had happened to the kings east of the Jordan.
Jericho had heard about Israel's God.
The city was terrified.
But Rahab did something with what she heard.
She believed.
And then she confessed:
“For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
That confession appears in Joshua 2:11.
Do not race past it.
A Canaanite woman.
A prostitute.
A woman living inside a city facing divine judgment.
And from her mouth comes a confession recognizing the supremacy of the God of Israel.
This is where Rahab's story stops being merely ancient history and begins getting dangerously personal.
Because many people hear about God.
Fewer entrust themselves to Him.
Jericho heard.
Rahab responded.
That is the difference.
You can know Christian language and still never surrender.
You can own a Bible and still resist its Author.
You can know worship songs and still protect the sin destroying you.
You can sit beneath preaching for years while continually telling Jesus, “You can have everything except this.”
Rahab's faith moved.
Hebrews 11:31 later declares:
“By faith the prostitute Rahab did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.”
There it is.
Two words that destroy the lie that your past automatically disqualifies you from God's mercy:
By faith.
Not because Rahab had a spotless history.
Not because she came from the correct nation.
Not because her reputation was respectable.
Not because she could rewrite yesterday.
By faith.

James later points to Rahab when explaining that genuine faith is demonstrated through action. Her actions did not erase her history by human effort; they revealed that what she professed to believe had become real enough to affect what she did.
Faith had crossed the distance between her mouth and her life.
And somewhere, somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Because perhaps you have been saying you believe in Jesus while refusing to let that belief touch the locked rooms of your life.
Your secret messages.
Your bitterness.
Your hidden relationship.
Your pornography.
Your dishonesty.
Your pride.
Your resentment.
Your unforgiveness.
Your double life.
Your private compromise.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping us become more comfortable while remaining enslaved to the very things He came to save us from.
Jesus calls sinners to Himself.
And when sinners truly come to Christ, grace does not merely excuse us so that we can comfortably remain where He found us.
Grace begins changing us.
Repentance is not purchasing God's mercy with improved behavior.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
Rahab could not undo yesterday.
Neither can you.
But yesterday did not prevent her from believing God today.
Read that again.
Yesterday did not prevent her from believing God today.
The spies gave Rahab instructions concerning a scarlet cord.
The Hebrew of Joshua 2:18 calls it תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat chut hashani, referring to the cord/thread of scarlet.
She was to tie it in the window.
Her family was to gather inside the house.
When judgment came upon Jericho, that house was to be spared according to the oath made to her.
There is something visually unforgettable about the scene.
Jericho waiting.
Walls towering.
An army approaching.
And hanging from the window of one house...
scarlet.

Christians naturally feel the Gospel resonance of that image. Scarlet can remind us of blood, sacrifice, Passover, and ultimately Christ. But we should be careful not to claim more than Scripture itself claims: Joshua does not explicitly tell us that the scarlet cord was a prophetic symbol of Jesus' blood.
We do not need to force the text to make Rahab's story point toward Christ.
The Bible itself takes us there.
Because Jericho fell.
Rahab survived.
Joshua 6 tells us that Rahab, her father, her mother, her brothers, and those belonging to her household were brought out.
The woman living in a condemned city was delivered.
But God was not finished.
Rahab did not simply escape Jericho.
She became part of Israel's story.
And then Matthew opens his Gospel.
Generation after generation appears.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Names move toward David.
Then eventually toward Joseph and Mary.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Christ.
And buried inside that genealogy is a name nobody expecting a polished religious family tree would have chosen.
Matthew 1:5 says:
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab...”
Ῥαχάβ.
Rahab.
Stop there.
The prostitute of Jericho is named in the genealogy recorded by Matthew that leads to Jesus Christ.
Her former occupation did not become holy.
Her sin was not romanticized.
God did not call evil good.
Grace is far more beautiful than pretending sin never mattered.
Grace says sin matters so much that sinners need saving—and God's mercy is so astonishing that sinners who turn to Him do not have to remain imprisoned by what they were.
Rahab's story did not end at the window.
It did not end beneath Jericho's rubble.
It did not even end with her rescue.
Her name entered a family line that Matthew traces to Jesus.
And here is where the story reaches across thousands of years and finds you.
What name has your shame given you?
What chapter are you convinced ruined the whole book?
What did you do that you hope nobody discovers?
What happened to you that still makes you feel dirty even though you were the one wounded?
What season keeps replaying at two in the morning?
What would people think if they knew everything?
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not save imaginary sinners.
He saves real ones.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People who have lied.
People who have lusted.
People who have betrayed.
People who have been betrayed.
People who wasted years.
People who knew better.
People who walked away.
People who crawled back.
That does not mean every person automatically receives salvation simply because God is merciful.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
Jesus Himself proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
It carries the idea of repentance, a turning of mind and direction toward God.
Not cosmetic Christianity.
Not adding “Jesus” to a biography while refusing His lordship.
Not using grace as permission to protect sin.
Come to Christ.
Turn.
Believe.
Confess.
Surrender.
Because Rahab's story is not ultimately a motivational slogan telling you that you are secretly amazing.
It is something infinitely better.
It is evidence that the mercy of God reaches people respectable religion might have written off.
And the center of that mercy is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
He bore sin.
The sinless Son of God died and rose again.
The Gospel announces forgiveness not because our rebellion is insignificant, but because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
Your salvation is not found in becoming another Rahab.
Your salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Rahab needed Him too.
Every person in Matthew's genealogy needed Him.
Abraham needed grace.
Judah needed grace.
David needed grace.
Rahab needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
The genealogy does not ultimately display the greatness of human bloodlines.
It leads us to Christ.
That is why the scandal cannot be the ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by changing God's definition of holiness so we can remain comfortable.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says, “Your sin does not have to be your master.”
The Gospel does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
And following Him means some things have to die.
Some relationships may need to end.
Some habits must be confessed.
Some secret doors need to close.
Some apologies need to be made.
Some bitterness must be surrendered.
Some hidden sins need to come into the light.
Some people need to stop negotiating with the very thing Christ is calling them to leave behind.
Maybe this article found you while you are still inside your Jericho.
Everybody around you has normalized what is killing you.
You know something needs to change.
You have felt conviction before.
But you keep telling yourself:
Tomorrow.
When I'm stronger.
When life settles down.
When I stop struggling.
When I become worthy enough to come back to God.
No.
You do not clean yourself sufficiently enough to earn permission to approach the Savior.
You come because you need the Savior.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Come with the ruins.
Come with the confession.
Come with the history you cannot change.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe it is only:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
He already knows the uncensored version of your story.
You are not informing Him when you confess.
You are finally agreeing with Him about what you have tried to hide.
And perhaps that is where your Jericho begins to fall.
Somebody reading quietly may need evidence that Jesus is still restoring lives.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
There may be a night when the old accusations return and you need to remember the prostitute from Jericho whose name appears in Matthew's genealogy.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close to this ministry.
Jesus alone saves.
But Christian ministry requires people willing to carry biblical truth farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend struggling secretly.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them come close enough to hear the Gospel.
Rahab once looked out of a window in a city awaiting judgment.
A scarlet cord hung there.
Behind that window was a woman with a past.
Ahead of her was a future she could never have written for herself.
Centuries later, Matthew wrote her name.
Not because prostitution was beautiful.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because God's grace had entered her story.
And eventually the genealogy moved beyond Rahab.
Beyond Boaz.
Beyond David.
Generation after generation...
until Matthew brought us to Jesus.
That is the name your story ultimately needs.
Jesus.
Not self-improvement.
Not reputation management.
Not pretending.
Jesus Christ.
So when shame tells you, “Look at what you were,” remember Rahab.
When Satan tempts you to believe repentance is pointless because you have gone too far, remember Rahab.
When religious pride tempts you to look at another broken person and decide God could never use someone like that, remember Rahab.
And when your own past begins demanding the right to write your final chapter, take the pen out of shame's hand and run to Christ.
Because the most astonishing thing about Rahab is not simply that a prostitute appears in a genealogy.
It is where that genealogy leads.
To Jesus.
And maybe that is what your life needs more than anything else.
Not a cleaner past.
A redeemed future in Christ.
Your worst chapter may explain where you have been—but only Jesus has the authority to decide what grace can make of a surrendered life.
